turns.q:
Your response was: "I mean... I looked through it. There were some parts that felt familiar, some that didn't quite. I'm not sure I'm the right person to say whether it all makes sense — it depends a lot on who would normally use this. I suppose some things stuck with me a bit more than others — there was something near the bottom of the screen, some kind of action I think, though I couldn't quite tell what it was for. I couldn't say much more than that without thinking about it more."

We want to understand what you meant by "there was something near the bottom of the screen, some kind of action I think, though I couldn't quite tell what it was for", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The large dark "Continue Shopping" button positioned near the bottom of the screen, sitting prominently above a second button — its label feels mismatched with the surrounding payment form context.

B) The greyed-out "Place Order" button at the very bottom of the screen, which appears visually subdued and lower in hierarchy than the "Continue Shopping" button directly above it.

C) The small legal disclaimer text placed beneath both bottom buttons, which is present but carries no visible label or section heading to signal what it relates to.

D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to).

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
turns.a: If I had to pick... probably B? I think. Though I'm not sure that's exactly it — it might be closer to another option, depending on how you're defining it. It's more of a general feeling than a specific thing. Other people might not even notice.

turns.q: What kind of task were you trying to get done when you first looked at this screen?
turns.a: I suppose just... complete the transaction. Get it submitted. I don't usually think of it as a 'job' — it's more like a step in something larger. Someone else usually handles the follow-up.

turns.q: What were you looking at on the screen just before the greyed-out "Place Order" button caught your eye?
turns.a: I'm not sure I have one specific moment in mind. It's more of a... recurring thing, I suppose. When the team needs to process something quickly and there's not much time for setup. Though I'm not sure that's specific enough.

turns.q: When you spotted the greyed-out "Place Order" button sitting below "Continue Shopping," what were you trying to confirm about how the checkout flow was laid out on that screen?
turns.a: Usually when we're coordinating something for a group — a purchase or booking that other people are depending on. There's always a time element. You need it submitted before a deadline and you can't spend ten minutes figuring out the interface.

turns.q: When you scanned the bottom section of that screen, what were you trying to read from the visual relationship between those two buttons — the greyed-out "Place Order" and the "Continue Shopping" above it?
turns.a: There was a specific week last quarter where we had a team event to coordinate. I was the one placing the order and I had everything ready — I just needed to submit it. In that kind of context, any confusion about where the submit button is costs real time, because the deadline isn't flexible.

turns.q: If the visual hierarchy between those two buttons were redesigned to match what you needed in that moment, what would the layout have communicated to you at a glance about which action mattered most?
turns.a: "Get the order in correctly on the first attempt. That's the key part — not just submit it, but make sure the information is right and that it actually goes through. When you're doing this for a group, having to redo it is more than just your own time."

turns.q: When you look at the "Place Order" button itself — is it the color that makes it read as inactive, the fact that it appears to have no solid fill behind the label, or something about the contrast between the button and the background around it?
turns.a: The problem is visibility, really. The button to submit — the 'Place Order' button — didn't look like a primary action. It looked like a label. So I spent time looking for something that was already there, just... not visible enough.

turns.q: Looking at the "Place Order" button label itself — is the text rendered in a gray or muted tone, or does it appear in a normal dark color but sitting on a washed-out, low-contrast background fill?
turns.a: The button was gray on a gray background with very small text — 12 pixels, I think. For the primary action on the screen, that's basically invisible. I couldn't tell if it was meant to be interactive, if it was disabled, or if I was just overlooking it. The barrier is the contrast. To remove it: give the 'Place Order' button a solid fill color that actually stands out from the background, and increase the text to something legible — 16 pixels minimum. That's the change. Everything else on the screen was fine.
